extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and educated readers seeking a moral/philosophical standard for evaluating and producing art
extracted.subtask_description: A prescriptive framework for judging and creating art according to Tolstoy's criterion that art should transmit feelings that unite people, grounded in the religious perception of the age (for Tolstoy, Christian brotherhood). Emphasises accessibility, subject-matter, and infection of feeling over purely technical or aesthetic concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of art — infection/transmission of feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is nothing but the infection by one man of another, or of others, with the feelings experienced by the infector; the more art fulfils that purpose the better the art, and the less it fulfils it the worse the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by their capacity to transmit (infect) genuine feelings from artist to audience. Technical virtuosity, beauty, or novelty are secondary; what matters is whether the spectator is moved to feel what the artist felt. Examples/notes: Tolstoy repeatedly asserts this as the fundamental characteristic of art; a work that fails to infect is not real art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appraisal by the religious perception of the age
rubrics_metrics.description: The appraisement of feelings (i.e. the acknowledgment of these or those feelings as being more or less good) is made by the religious perception of the age; art should be appraised on the basis of this religious perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge subject-matter against the dominant moral/life-conception (religious perception) of the society. Art transmitting feelings that make that perception operative in life should be chosen and encouraged; art transmitting feelings contrary to it should be condemned. Anti-pattern: praising art simply because it conforms to earlier or foreign religious perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of 'religious perception'
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious perception in a society is the understanding of the meaning of life which represents the highest level to which men of that society have attained; it is the guide to the direction of progress and by its standard the feelings transmitted by art have always been estimated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the rubric, first identify the relevant religious perception (the era's guiding life-conception). For Tolstoy's time this is articulated as the consciousness of brotherhood and loving harmony among all men. Use that perception to decide whether feelings transmitted by art are 'good' or 'bad' in subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should promote brotherhood/unity (subject-matter criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The religious perception of our time ... is the consciousness that our well-being ... lies in the growth of brotherhood among all men — in their loving harmony with one another. Art transmitting feelings flowing from this religious perception should be chosen, prized, and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work's subject-matter and evoked feelings tend to unite people (promote compassion, self-sacrifice, mutual love) rather than divide them. Works that foster empathy, pity, humility, devotion, and mutual regard are positively valued. Example: Christian art that evokes love of God and neighbour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / accessibility of feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Christian art of our time must be such that all men can experience the feelings it transmits; it must not transmit feelings which are accessible only to a man educated in a certain way, or only to an aristocrat, or a merchant, or only to a Russian, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key test is whether people across classes, nations, ages, and educations can equally feel what the art expresses. If comprehension or emotional response requires special training or cultural membership, the art is exclusive (bad) for Tolstoy’s standard. Examples/anti-patterns: much celebrated 'upper-class' art, symbolic pictures, and elite music are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of good art (religious and universal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Christian art of our time can be of two kinds: (1) art transmitting feelings flowing from a religious perception of man’s position in the world in relation to God and to his neighbour (religious art); and (2) art transmitting the simplest feelings of common life, accessible to everyone (universal art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a work, determine whether it belongs to religious art (evoking devotion, self-sacrifice, moral indignation at violation of love) or to universal art (everyday feelings like merriment, pity, tranquillity). Both are legitimate if they unite people. Note which forms favour each: religious art often in words/painting/sculpture; universal art can appear in all arts, especially music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude exclusive/divisive subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of our time excludes from the domain of art good in subject-matter everything transmitting exclusive feelings, which do not unite but divide men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark as bad art those works promoting patriotism that divides, church-specific cult art, aristocratic/idle-rich feelings (satiety, spleen), erotically voluptuous subjects, and any art whose emotional content is particular to a class or clique. Examples: patriotic anthems that incite division, symbolic art understandable only within a circle, erotic nudity dominating galleries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint of detail to preserve universality
rubrics_metrics.description: All details, except the most essential ... are superfluous, and would only hinder the transmission of feelings; the subject-matter must be strong enough that superfluous detail is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simplicity and omission of extraneous, local or time-bound particulars that impede universal comprehension. Example: the Biblical story of Joseph is highly universal because it avoids superfluous descriptive detail; many modern novels are spoiled by 'realism' or 'provincialism' that limits their universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and technique must serve infectious feeling, not replace it
rubrics_metrics.description: Anxiety about the technique and the beauty of the picture for the most part obscures the feeling... Art remains what it was and what it must be: nothing but the infection by one man of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept technical mastery or aesthetic ornamentation as sufficient; evaluate whether formal excellence enhances or obscures the emotional transmission. Anti-patterns: highly finished historical paintings that emphasize spectacle over feeling (Gérôme’s 'Pollice Verso').

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-specific accessibility: melody vs complex harmonisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody—every melody—is free, and may be understood of all men; but as soon as it is bound up with a particular harmony, it ceases to be accessible except to people trained to such harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging music, favor simple, memorable melodies that can be grasped by all; be wary of complex harmonic/rhythmic/orchestral complications that restrict comprehension to a trained elite. Examples of universally accessible bits: Bach aria, Chopin nocturne; critics of Wagner, Liszt, Strauss as exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamentation and 'simple' arts can be legitimate art
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of all kinds of ornamentation consists not in the beauty, but in the feeling ... which the artist has experienced and with which he infects the spectator. Ornaments ... are intelligible to everyone and evoke a similar feeling of admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss applied arts, ornaments, genre objects, landscapes, or folk art as lesser by default. If they genuinely transmit a feeling accessible to many, they qualify as good art under this criterion. Example: china dolls, Yakutsk ornaments, Greek ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for evaluating a work (three-step test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the work may be ... we have first to ask whether this work is one of real art or a counterfeit. ... it is necessary, on the basis of the indication of its accessibility, to decide the next question, Does this work belong to the category of bad, exclusive art ... or to Christian art, uniting people?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply a stepwise evaluation: (1) Is it real art (does it infect anyone)? (2) Is it accessible/universal or exclusive? (3) If accessible, is it religious art (transmitting love of God/neighbour) or universal art (simple common feelings)? Use this procedure to select works that supply necessary spiritual food and to reject harmful counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences criterion — art as organ of human progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is one of two organs of human progress. ... the perversion of either of them must cause evil results: first, the absence ... of the work which should be performed by the organ; and secondly, the harmful activity of the perverted organ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider social consequences: good art furthers human progress and spiritual life (union, moral improvement); perverted or exclusive art wastes labour, corrupts sensibilities, deprives society of beneficial influence, and may foster cruelty or division. Use societal impact as an additional evaluative lens.
